issues.legal_issue: A partition of joint Hindu family property is not a transfer of property in the strict legal sense.
material_facts: A joint Hindu family divided its property among its coparceners.
One coparcener received property worth less than the property allotted to the other members.
The dispute arose in a gift-tax proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The partition did not effect a transfer of property in the strict sense.
issues.legal_principle: A partition transforms joint enjoyment into enjoyment in severalty; each coparcener has an antecedent title, so no new title is conferred by conveyance. The Court followed Commissioner of Income-tax, Gujarat v. Keshavlal Lallubhai Patel, which discussed Gutta Radhakrishnavya v. Gutta Sarasamma, M. K. Stremann v. Commissioner of Income-tax, and Jagan Nath v. State of Punjab.

predicates.gift_tax_proceeding: The dispute concerns whether a transaction in a gift-tax proceeding is taxable as a gift.
predicates.joint_family_property_partition: Members of a joint family divided jointly held family property among themselves.

issues.definition: When a gift-tax proceeding concerns a partition of joint family property, the partition is not treated as a strict transfer of property.

issues.legal_issue: A joint Hindu family partition in which a coparcener takes less than the other members does not constitute a taxable gift where the coparcener had no definite share in the property before partition.
material_facts: The family property was divided among a coparcener and other family members, with the coparcener taking less property than the others.
Before partition, the coparcener had no definite share in the joint family property.
The record did not establish a division of status before the properties were divided.
The issue arose under the statutory definition of gift and transfer of property.
issues.conclusion: The partition was not a transfer within the extended statutory definition and did not amount to a gift liable to gift tax.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(xii) and 2(xxiv) of the Gift Tax Act, 1958, a gift requires a transfer of property. The listed modes of transfer in section 2(xxiv) are to be understood in their statutory context and do not encompass a partition. Clause (d) also does not apply where a coparcener had no definite share before partition and therefore cannot be said to have diminished the value of his own property or increased another's; the transaction in that clause takes its meaning from the main clause and must involve a transfer of property. Section 3 charges tax on gifts. The Court relied on Commissioner of Income-tax, Gujarat v. Keshavlal Lallubhai Patel and the contextual approach to interpretation discussed in Craies on Statute Law.

rule.if: gift_tax_proceeding and joint_family_property_partition and coparcener_had_no_definite_prepartition_share and coparcener_took_less_than_other_members and no_prior_status_division_shown

predicates.gift_tax_proceeding: The dispute concerns whether a transaction in a gift-tax proceeding is taxable as a gift.
predicates.joint_family_property_partition: Members of a joint family divided jointly held family property among themselves.
predicates.coparcener_had_no_definite_prepartition_: A coparcener had no definite individual share in the joint family property before it was divided.
predicates.coparcener_took_less_than_other_members: A coparcener received less property than the other members received in the partition.
predicates.no_prior_status_division_shown: The evidence did not establish that the family’s status had been divided before the property was divided.

issues.definition: If a gift-tax proceeding concerns a joint family partition in which a coparcener had no definite prior share, took less than the other members, and no earlier division of status was shown, the partition is not treated as a taxable gift.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal relying on a certificate unsupported by reasons is not maintainable when the certificate does not sustain the appeal.
material_facts: One appeal was brought on the strength of a certificate granted by the High Court.
The certificate was unsupported by any reason.
A separate appeal concerning the same judgment was brought by special leave.
issues.conclusion: The appeal based on the unsupported certificate was dismissed as not maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the certificate as insufficient to sustain the appeal because it was unsupported by any reason; no earlier case or statutory provision was cited for this procedural conclusion.

predicates.appeal_based_on_high_court_certificate: An appeal was brought on the basis of a certificate granted by a High Court.
predicates.certificate_unsupported_by_reasons: The certificate supporting the appeal was not accompanied by reasons.

issues.definition: An appeal brought on a High Court certificate unsupported by reasons is not maintainable.
